en: The Vajraśekhara-kūṭāgāra-sarvayoginī-tantra, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śramaṇa Vajrabodhi of South India during the Tang Dynasty.
Chapter One: The Introduction Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Bhagavān, the Tathāgata Vajradhātuvairocana, by means of the four kinds of *dharmakāya* formed from the five wisdoms, within the primordial, self-awakened Great Samaya of Sovereignty in the Primordial Vajradhātu— (Note:
The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)
Within the heart-palace of the indestructible vajra-light of the Bodhicitta— the full moon of Samantabhadra— together with the retinue of self-nature,
the sixteen great bodhisattvas such as Vajrapāṇi, the four goddesses of the means of attraction,
and the eight vajra goddesses of inner and outer offerings, each empower [the assembly] through their respective original vows.
Holding [the mudrā], one abides in the vajra-moon disc, maintaining the insignia of the fundamental samādhi.
All, by means of the subtle dharmakāya and the secret ground of mind, transcend the vajras of body, speech, and mind of the ten stages.
Each, through the light-peaks of the five wisdoms, manifests five hundred million koṭis of subtle vajras, which completely fill space.
The *dharmadhātu* cannot be seen by Bodhisattvas of any stage, nor is it fully realized by them;

yet its blazing radiance and sovereign power constantly manifest unimpeded transformation bodies throughout the three times to benefit and bring happiness to sentient beings without even a moment’s rest,
through various enlightened activities that are pure and unstained, universally illuminating with the light of the vajra-like intrinsic nature.
He then empowered himself to save and deliver sentient beings, proclaiming that the Vajrayāna is the sole Vajra capable of severing afflictions.
By means of this profound and secret ground of the mind—the self-nature of Samantabhadra, the eternally abiding Dharmakāya—he gathered all Bodhisattvas;
this alone exhausts the benefits of the Buddhas. It is the Guhyasamāja and the Avataṃsaka, accomplished through the purity of the vajra self-nature.
It is accomplished through the fulfillment of the provisions of merit and wisdom for sentient beings by means of the practices and vows of great compassion;
it is the body of equalizing wisdom that eternally abides throughout the three times, never ceasing for a moment, illuminated by the light of the five wisdoms.

At that time, the sixteen great bodhisattvas, including Samantabhadra and Vajrapāṇi, arose from their meditative absorption. Pervading the void with the vajra-nature of self-accomplished pure radiance, they praised him in unison with these verses:
“Mahāvairocana, Vajra-Peak, Subtle, abiding in spontaneity, Your light constantly shines everywhere; Unfailing is your pure activity.”

Having spoken these praises, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi cast his five-pronged vajra into the sky with his right hand; it remained in silent unity and returned to rest within his hand. He uttered this vajra-syllable: “HŪṂ.
Then the Bodhisattva Vajrarāja cast the hook he held into the sky; it remained in silent unity and returned to rest within his hand. He uttered this maṇi-syllable: “TRAḤ.
Then the Bodhisattva Vajrarāga cast the white lotus of the vajra into the sky; it remained in silent unity and returned to rest within his hand. He uttered this lotus-syllable: [PADMA].
When “Hrīḥ” was uttered, the Bodhisattva Vajraghoṣa cast a vajra-vīṇā into the void; it became silent and returned as one with his body, remaining in his hand. He then spoke this *karma-mantra*: “Aḥ.
At that time, the four great Bodhisattvas spoke with one voice to the Tathāgata Vajradhātu:

“We now manifest these supernatural powers in order to stir the fundamental nature of all sentient beings, to reveal and summon those foolish children, to cause them to be imbued with love for the sublime Dharma of the Buddhas, and to bring to maturity their originally existent *dharmakāya*.”
Then, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha again cast the precious flask from his hand into space; it returned to his hand in a state of silent unity, and he uttered this Vajra-essence:
“Jaḥ. Then, the Bodhisattva Sūryaprabha cast the solar disc from his hand into space; it returned to his hand in a state of silent unity, and he uttered this Vajra-light:
“Hūṃ. Then, the Bodhisattva Gaganaketu cast the banner from his hand into space; it returned to his hand in a state of silent unity, and he uttered this Vajra-banner:

When the syllable “VAṂ” was uttered, the Bodhisattva Ākāśasmita cast a vajra-banner from his hand into the void; it returned silently as a single entity into his hand, and he spoke this vajra-banner: “HAḤ.
At that time, the four great bodhisattvas spoke with one voice to the Tathāgata Vajradhātu, saying:

“We now manifest these supernatural powers because we wish to summon all sentient beings and cause them to enter the Dharma-realm; by means of the hook, we draw them to the Vajra-field; by means of the chain, we firmly bind the gaṇas; and by means of the bell, we gladden their nature so that they may experience bliss.”

Then, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara cast the mirror from his hand into the void; it remained silent as a single entity and returned to rest within his hand. He then uttered this Vajra-wisdom: "Āḥ" (with the high tone).

Then, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī cast the *bhr̥ṅgāra* (water-pitcher) from his hand into the void; it remained silent as a single entity and returned to rest within his hand. He then uttered the Mani-practice: "Ā" (prolonged).
Then, the Bodhisattva Dharmacakrapravartin cast the wheel from his hand into the void; it remained silent as a single entity and returned to rest within his hand. He then uttered the Lotus-samādhi:
When the syllable *Aṃ* was uttered, the Bodhisattva Vajrasvara threw the conch from his hand into the void; it remained silent as a single essence and returned to rest within his hand.
He then spoke this *karma-mantra*: "Aḥ. At that time, the four Great Bodhisattvas spoke with one voice to the Tathāgata Vajradhātu:

"We now manifest these supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) because we wish to reveal the primordially non-arising nature inherent in all sentient beings, to cause the fulfillment of the myriad practices through cultivation, to bring about the attainment of Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), and to enter the immovable wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*)."

Then, the Bodhisattva Vajrakarma cast a green jewel from his hand into the void; it remained silent as a single entity and returned to rest within his hand. He spoke this yoga: “Ī (prolonged, with the departing tone).
Then, the Bodhisattva Vajrarakṣa cast a parasol from his hand into the void; it remained silent as a single entity and returned to rest within his hand. He spoke this yoga: “Ī (prolonged).
Then, the Bodhisattva Vajrachattra cast a *karmamukha* from his hand into the void; it remained silent as a single entity and returned to rest within his hand. He spoke this yoga:

When [the syllable] *Hūṃ* was uttered, the Bodhisattva Vajradhara cast the moon from his hand into the void; it became silent and of one essence, returning to rest within his hand. He then spoke this yoga:
"When [the syllable] *Auḥ* (in the rising tone) was uttered, the four great bodhisattvas spoke with one voice to the Tathāgata Vajradhātu:

'We now manifest this supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) because we wish to give birth to all phenomena so that all sentient beings may enjoy them according to their needs; because we wish to accomplish the three bodies (*trikāya*) of the Tathāgata; because we wish to accomplish the bodies of all sentient beings throughout the pervasive realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); and because we wish to attain the bliss of mastery within saṃsāra.'"

At that time, the Tathāgatas of the four directions, desiring to manifest and realize the primordially present vajra-nature of all Tathāgatas, spoke in unison these four kinds of one-syllable secret heart-mantras:

“HŪṂ. Then the four Bodhisattvas of the Pāramitās, desiring to benefit all sentient beings by practicing the vows and conduct of great compassion, spoke in unison these four kinds of one-syllable expedient yoga of the heart:

“OṂ. Then the inner offering goddesses and messengers, desiring to manifest the internal supernatural powers of the Tathāgatas through offerings such as joyous garlands, song, and dance, spoke in unison these four kinds of one-syllable vajra-hearts:

When [the syllable] “Hak” (鵠) is uttered, the female messengers who serve as external offerings, desiring to cause the conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*) of all sentient beings to be swiftly perfected, speak these four kinds of one-syllable hearts:
When “Hūṃ” (吽) is uttered, the female messengers at the four gates, desiring to lead all sentient beings into the palace of the *dharmadhātu*, speak these four kinds of one-syllable hearts in unison:
When “Hūṃ” (吽) is uttered, the Tathāgata Vajradhātu further speaks the secret mantra of the one-syllable heart of Samantabhadra of the *stūpa* and the *dharmadhātu*:
“BĀṂ. At that time, the Tathāgata Vajradhātu again addressed Vajrapāṇi, saying:

“If there are sons or daughters of good family who receive and maintain this profound and secret Yoga of the Great Victorious Vajra Mind of All Tathāgatas—the yoga of accomplishment of the thirty-seven deities who possess the noble self-awakened wisdom—they should employ the accomplishment of the thirty-seven karma-mudrās within the Vajradhātu. They should constantly hold the single-syllable heart-mantra of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, making it correspond with the breath through inhalation and exhalation. Through the vajra-wisdom of body, speech, and mind, they shall swiftly attain it and swiftly realize the body of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra. This is called the profound and secret correspondence of the thirty-seven wisdoms of the Samantabhadra Bodhisattva Vajrasattva Samaya; the Great Ācārya should perform this rite.”

If any ācāryas have previously entered the Great Empowerment of the Vajradhātu and have received the rank of Vajradhātu-ācārya, they should practice this method; by constantly aligning the three karmas with the single syllable, they shall attain the body of the Great Samantabhadra-sattva.
At that time, the Tathāgata Samantabhadra of the Vajradhātu spoke in verse of praise:
"Great is the vajra-nature, The King whose radiance shines everywhere;
Pure and unstained by the wondrous lotus, He performs his deeds without effort."
The Vajra Hook arises, blazing with majesty throughout the three realms;
it decisively dispels the darkness of ignorance.
Clad in the adamantine armor, it brings peace, happiness, and further benefit to all sentient beings who are subject to desire.
Turning the wheel of Dharma at will, completely eliminating all veils and hindrances;
praising others to bring them joy, whether through playful laughter or pleasing discourse;
transcending words yet capable of such deeds, my three karmas are ever-abiding in tranquility.
The Vidyādhara Ācārya, contemplating the sixteen meanings and reciting the single-syllable heart-mantra, completes the thirty-seven [perfections];
always upholding this King of Praises and binding the Great Karma-mudrā.
If one constructs a maṇḍala, paints an image of yoga,
or forms the stūpa mudrā, one should recite the vidyā at the four locations.
For the Samaya of Samantabhadra, bend the forefinger like a hook.
The union of generosity, wisdom, meditation, and knowledge—this is called the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā).
Next, recite the one-syllable vidyā and bind the Great Karma Seal;
doing so continuously from time to time, the thirty-seven [auxiliaries] will be perfected.

Chapter Two: The Heart-Mind of the King of Firm Attachment to the Profound Meaning of the Supreme Vajra Sovereign of All Tathāgatas. At that time, the Blessed One again entered the *samādhi* of the Horse-Hide Secret Organ (*aśvakośa*). It was the profound, hidden, and deeply tranquil state of all Tathāgatas, blazing with fierce intensity, heroic, wrathful, and majestic. It produced sounds such as the lion’s roar, the quivering of lightning, the sound of celestial drums, the cry of the fragrant elephant king, the great vajra-sound, and the great conch-shell sound. These and other such sounds resounded.
At that time, the Bodhisattvas Vajrapāṇi, Vajradhara, and others, having seen such signs, praised him with one voice, saying:
"The Buddhas are most extraordinary; The thundering sound of the vajra— What Dharma teaching do you wish to proclaim? We pray that the Tathāgata will expound it."
Then the Tathāgata Vajradhātu addressed Vajrapāṇi and the others, saying: “Vajrapāṇi!

There is a mantra named ‘The Heart Mantra of the King of Passion, Firm in Purpose and Meaning, the Supreme Sovereign of All Tathāgatas. It is the most honored and supreme among all yogas; it swiftly grants siddhi, and causes all who see it to conceive of [the practitioner] as their father, mother, wife, or son. Whatever karma one performs shall be accomplished. Furthermore, regarding all other mantras one may hold—whether those of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa family, the various Tathāgata families, the Padma family, the Vajra family, or the Karma family—one can suppress those mantras and cause them to be swiftly accomplished.”

If a practitioner of mantras recites this sūtra three hundred thousand times, all the lords of mantras and the Great Maṇḍala Kings of the Vajradhātu will assemble; they will simultaneously grant accomplishment, and one shall swiftly attain the rank of the Great Vajra, up to the rank of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
Then the World-Honored One spoke these words of explanation:
"Oṃ mahāra-kṣa-vajra-śani-ṣa-vajra-sattva-jña hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ. Then the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
"Form two vajra-fists with both hands; Interlace them and bind them within."
Upright the needles of patience and vow; when they intersect, they form the "dye.
This is called the Root Seal.
Furthermore, by the power of the secret seal, one seals the heart, forehead, throat, and crown.
Like the body of Vajraśekhara, all stains of sin are extinguished the moment the mudrā is formed.
For subjugation, reverence, or love, it acts according to that which is desired.
As soon as this mantra is recited, one shall immediately obtain [the desired result].
Whether it be poison or mutual hatred, they shall cease the moment the mudrā is formed and the recitation performed.
If one consecrates food seven times with this, I shall descend as nectar.

Chapter Three: The Chapter on the Station of the Great Ācārya of All Tathāgatas At that time, Vajradhātu Tathāgata again entered the samādhi called “The Eye of All Tathāgatas, Radiant with the Color of Light,” and further spoke this mantra for the station of the conduct of all ācāryas:

“Oṃ vajrasukṣama rakṣa rakṣa sattvātma hūṃ hūṃ. If a practitioner of mantra recites this daily for one month, they shall swiftly attain all the ritual activities practiced by all Ācāryas, as well as all wisdom, penetration of meaning, and skillful means. All Tathāgatas will constantly protect them, and Vajrasattva will always be their close friend, dwelling perpetually within the practitioner’s heart. Wherever they think of him, he will arrive; there will be no further need for laborious invocation, mudrās, mantras, and the like.

If one constantly maintains this mantra, all vidyās will be fully accomplished. The vidyādharas will always serve as minor attendants, and the kings of the *Yama*, Varuṇa, Agni, Vāyu, Vaiśravaṇa, Maheśvara, and Indra will constantly act as messengers to provide whatever is required. All wishes and desires will be swiftly attained, and before long, one shall attain the rank of a Great Vajrācārya and the body of Dharmatā Mahāvairocana. All who behold one will prostrate at one’s feet, bowing in joyful submission.

As for this mudrā: with the hands of concentration and wisdom, bend the elbows upward and join the palms level with the shoulders; bend the index fingers (śīla) and ring fingers (kṣānti) of each hand so they enter the palms. Whether sitting or standing, it is accomplished in both positions.

Chapter Four: The Bodhicitta of Vajrasattva At that time, the World-Honored One further proclaimed that all sentient beings inherently possess the vajra-light that shines everywhere; it is pure and unstained, primordially quiescent, eternally constant throughout the three periods of time without cessation, the true great awakening of the firm vajra-sattva, primordially tranquil yet blazingly radiant, observing the vajra-equality-nature of all sentient beings.
Then he spoke the mantra of the bodhicitta of Vajrasattva: "Oṃ vajra-guhyasamāja hūṃ. "Vajrapāṇi! [he said].
If there be one who maintains this mantra, they shall immediately become a first-born son of all Buddhas and a foremost leader among Samantabhadra’s retinue.

If one recites this mantra seven times every day, they shall behold the present-life manifestations of all Buddhas appearing to rescue and deliver sentient beings; such a person is named Mahāvajrasattva and is also called the Primordially Existing Vajra of Great Enlightenment.

If there are those who establish the Vajradhātu Maṇḍala, the Mahākaruṇā-garbha Maṇḍala, or the maṇḍalas of the various families nearby, and if they recite this mantra, all those kings of the maṇḍalas will draw near and honor the practitioner of vidyā.

Why is this? Because they are able to cultivate the power of the practices and vows of all Tathāgatas; because they substitute for the deeds of the Buddhas to rescue and deliver sentient beings; and because they are able to make offerings to all Buddhas.
The practice of the shared vows is for the sake of the *sattva* of equality regarding all phenomena.
As for its mudrā: interlace the two hands with the palms facing inward, and with each hand, join the *dhyāna* (ring) and *prajñā* (pinky) fingers with the *vajra* (forefinger) and *bala* (thumb).
Chapter Five: The King of Passion (Rāgarāja). At that time, Vajrapāṇi again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I shall now further explain the miscellaneous methods for the common accomplishment (*siddhi*) of the King of Passion by all Tathāgatas, as well as the method for painting his image.”

“Śāntika (pacification), Pauṣṭika (increase), Vaśīkaraṇa (subjugation through love), Ākarṣaṇa (attraction), Abhicāruka (subjugation by force), and so forth. Then the Bhagavān Samantaprabha addressed Vajrapāṇi, saying:

“I have already taught that which was practiced and studied by all the Tathāgatas; you should now extensively explain it for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to good sons and good daughters in the age of the final dharma.”
Then Vajrapāṇi spoke in verse:
"On the day of the constellation Mṛgaśiras during the bright fortnight, take a pure white cotton cloth and paint Rāgavajra,
whose body is colored like the radiance of the sun."
Abiding upon a blazing wheel, with three eyes gazing with fierce wrath, his topknot is adorned with a lion crown;
he has the form of a wrathful deity with sharp bristling hair.
Furthermore, a five-pronged hook is placed upon the head of the lion.
A five-colored floral topknot hangs down, and a celestial band covers the ears;
the left hand holds a golden bell, and the right grasps a five-pronged vajra.
His form and appearance are like those of a sattva, establishing all beings within the realm of sentient existence.
Next, holding a vajra bow in the left hand and grasping a vajra arrow in the right,
as if shooting at the light of the stars, one is able to accomplish the Great Passion Dharma;
the lower left hand holds that [arrow], while the right lotus hand is in the posture of striking.
All hosts with evil minds shall be swiftly extinguished, of this there is no doubt.
Adorning the body by binding and knotting various flower garlands and cords,
one assumes the full lotus posture (paryaṅka) and dwells upon a red lotus.
Beneath the lotus is a precious vase, from both sides of which various jewels issue forth.
Install the image to the west; the practitioner faces west and forms the Great Karma Mudrā while reciting the root mantra.
Furthermore, he reveals the samaya and the single-syllable heart-mantra,
which can accomplish and utterly extinguish all multitudes of evil minds.
Again, he binds the Vajradhātu and performs the thirty-seven karmas.
And by means of the light of one's fundamental karma, one swiftly accomplishes hundreds of thousands of tasks;
all *ṇṛtya* [spirits], as well as the *graha*,
shall be subdued through wrathful rites in a single night.
Recite the root mantra and bind the samaya mudrā;
furthermore, have the gāthāya take the filaments of a red lotus and perform one hundred and eight homas.
After one night, there will be immediate attraction.
Furthermore, cause him to subdue [the obstacle] by carving a white sandalwood image of Vajrarāgarāja, five finger-widths in measurement;
wearing it constantly upon his person, he shall [subdue] all classes of sentient beings.
As well as all Kṣatriya kings, he subdues them like servants.
Constantly forming the Karma-mudrā and reciting the Great Root Vidyā,
he increases all merit, becoming as firm and solid as a vajra.
If the seven planets oppress one’s destiny, karma, or natal signs,
one should draw their forms and names and place them within the mouth of a lion;
by reciting [the mantra] one thousand and eight times, they will be swiftly extinguished and shall not arise again.
Even unto Śakra and Brahmā, the lords, and the deities of water, fire, wind, and Yama;
the wicked classes who travel on their heads, roaming through boundless directions at night—
all these evil races shall tremble before the assembly of bhikṣus of pure conduct.
"The difficult-to-tame, venomous, and evil dragon, Nārāyaṇa, Īśvara,
and the four world-protecting Heavenly Kings— May they swiftly remove [the poison] and cause it to take his life.
He further spoke of King Rāgarāja.
The One-Syllable Heart Mantra says:
"Next, explain the fundamental mudrā: with both hands in the vajra-bond, join the middle and ring fingers together;
the thumbs and index fingers form the shape of a hook."
The *dāna-huì* (generosity-wisdom) and *chán-zhì* (meditation-wisdom) fingers are joined vertically like five peaks;
this is called the *karmamudrā*, and it is also called the *samaya*.
If one performs this binding even once and recites the fundamental mantra, [the result is attained].
It can extinguish immeasurable sins and generate immeasurable merit;
through the *śāntika* and other rites, the four matters are swiftly perfected.
Within the three times and the three realms, nothing can surpass it.
This is named the Vajra King, the most supreme name upon the crown;
the Samādhi of Vajrasattva, the mother of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, it explains the śāntika rite, conjoined with the five mudrās.
The fingers of the *śīla* hand enter the palms and interlace; *dhyāna* and *prajñā* hook and bind one another.
*Dāna* and *prajñā* join like needles; *kṣānti* and *praṇidhāna* are held upright and pressed together.
*Vīrya* and *bala* are each bent and then extended upward; this is called the Seal of the Quelling of Calamities (*śāntivyasanamudrā*).
With the *vajra-muṣṭi* (fist) of the *tarjanī* and *anāmikā* fingers, the tips of the four fingers aligned together—
this is the *vaśīkaraṇa* mudrā, the great seal of the Mātṛkā.
With the *tarjanī* finger like a lotus petal— this mudrā is named Gāthāyā.
Pressing the *tarjanī* and *anāmikā* fingers together, with the upper joints constricted into a triangle—
this secret mudrā should be employed for *āveśaruṣaka*.
Bending the *tarjanī* like a hook, one should summon [the deity] while reciting the mantra.
The Vajra-Aṅkuśa performs its activity at all times.
The Great Passion, the Vajra-Apex—thus the five secret mudrās have been explained.

Chapter Six: The Method for Subsuming the Four Practices of Yoga, Everywhere, for the Supreme Illuminator King of All Buddha-Uṣṇīṣas, the Ultimate Indestructible Destroyer of Evil. At that time, Vajrapāṇi again spoke the mantra of universal non-incompatibility:
"Oṃ vajrasattvaja hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ. He then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Regarding these four practices that encompass all phenomena, in every place and in every matter—whether it be worldly attachment and affection or any worldly phenomenon—one should conceive of them as the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), giving rise to the hook of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), the lure of compassion (*karuṇā*), the bond of joy (*muditā*), and the equanimity of impartiality (*upekṣā*).

In all matters and situations, one should give rise to these four methods of attraction (saṃgrahavastu). Within the vehicles of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, one should constantly initiate these four practices, recite the mantras of the four attractions, and form the four kinds of hook-seals (aṅkuśamudrā). These four hooks are as follows: regarding all beings with loving-kindness through the eyes; regarding all beings with compassion through the eyes; regarding all beings with sympathetic joy through the eyes; and regarding all beings with equanimity through the eyes.

The practitioner of mantra-mantras should constantly give rise to four kinds of mind; by performing all worldly activities without transgression, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi. In this very life, they shall manifest a body that realizes the equality of all phenomena—non-dual, unstained, neither pure nor impure, non-contradictory, and unimpeded—and abide eternally in the samādhi of Vajrasattva. By means of these four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), they shall extensively bring about the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.

"However, regarding all matters and situations, one should give rise to a state of non-opposition; employing these four methods of the eye, one should constantly, at all times, initiate the destruction of the minds of those of the Two Vehicles.
He then recited this mantra for destroying the minds of the Two Vehicles:

“Oṃ mahāvajratattvasarvadharmaviśodhane hūṃ. By constantly reciting this mantra, at all times, one should observe one’s own mind, destroy all attachments, and contemplate that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are primordially pure. Through this, merit increases, and in this very life, one attains the purity of all phenomena, the vajra-nature of the Vajrayāna, and an increase in all merit. One is constantly protected by all Tathāgatas, and all Vajras constantly shatter one's karma, causing one to realize the state of the Great Vajra in this very life.

Chapter Seven: The Chapter on the Accomplishment of the Yoga of the Great Victorious Vajra Mind of All Tathāgatas. At that time, Vajrapāṇi further spoke the one-syllable heart-mantra of the great victorious mind for the accomplishment of Vajrasattva, and uttered this mantra:

HŪṂ SUSIDDHI Furthermore, if one constantly recites and maintains this mantra, one will gain the love, respect, and subjugation of all devas and humans; it causes all who see one to rejoice; it accomplishes all heart-wishes so that they are entirely fulfilled; and one quickly attains the *siddhi* of the body of Vajrasattva. In this present life, one shall obtain the vajra-mind of the equality of all dharmas.
At that time, the bodhisattvas of the various stages within the assembly each used their supernatural powers and the majestic radiance of their merit to praise Vajrapāṇi, speaking these verses:
"That which all bodhisattvas Are unable to see or hear—
Now you proclaim this teaching of the Dharma, Skillfully understanding the secrets of our minds."
"All phenomena lack intrinsic nature; they are without aspiration, and neither defiled nor pure.
With the single vehicle of the Vajra, the teaching of all phenomena remains indestructible.

At that time, suddenly within the assembly, there appeared a hindrance that did not arise from space, nor come from another direction, nor emerge from the earth, yet it manifested instantaneously. All the bodhisattvas were as if intoxicated, not knowing its place of origin.
At that time, the Bhagavān smiled from his countenance and addressed Vajrapāṇi and the assembly of Bodhisattvas, saying:
"From where does this obstruction come?

It comes from the beginningless and unawakened state of the obstructions inherently present in all sentient beings; it is the obstruction co-emergent with the primordial nature, the obstruction produced by the self, and the primordial wheel of both the beginningless and the original limit."

At that time, the Obstructor suddenly manifested his form, appearing in the shape of Vajrasattva. A vajra-wheel appeared upon his crown, another vajra-wheel appeared beneath his feet, and a vajra-wheel appeared in each of his two hands. Furthermore, a vajra-wheel appeared upon his heart, and light radiated from his entire body, illuminating and touching all the great bodhisattvas in the assembly.
Then Vajrapāṇi addressed the Buddha:
"O Bhagavān, Universal Illuminator, I now wish to speak this self-arisen Vajraśekhara Dharma of Obstructions; I only pray that you will grant me permission to explain it."
Then Vajrapāṇi, receiving the holy command of the Buddha, spoke in verse:
“If there are mantra-practitioners who maintain the method of reciting mantras,
yet possess even a single distracted thought, this obstacle will immediately find its opportunity.”
It can seize away the meritorious deeds cultivated by a mantra master.
If one maintains the King of Passion, the fundamental single-syllable heart-mantra,
these obstacles will be swiftly extinguished, and [the practitioner] shall not suffer even the slightest proximity [to them].
Constantly within one's own mind, observe the sound of the single syllable HŪṂ;
as it enters and exits with the breath, neither body nor mind is perceived.
Observe only that which arises from the cause of the syllable, which is identical to the great emptiness.
Firmly abiding in the vajra-nature, one becomes entirely a vajra-body;
by swiftly transforming one’s own limbs, they become identical to a solid, adamantine body.
Like the mist of the eighth month of autumn, it is a subtle and pure light.
Abiding constantly in these meditative absorptions is called the subtle concentration.
Regarding the obstacles produced by one's own nature, if one lacks this skillful means,
they will certainly be like a vajra, such that none in the three realms can transcend them.
At that time, having heard these words, Svabhāvāvaraṇa suddenly vanished. Chapter Eight:

The Supreme Reality of the Great Samaya of the Supreme Vajraśekhara of All Tathāgatas. Then the Bhagavān Vairocana again manifested various kinds of light; from his crown he emitted the light of the vajra-ferocity, illuminating all the bodhisattvas, while Vajrapāṇi and the others remained each silent.

Again, he manifested his own body with twelve arms, holding the Wisdom Fist Seal (*jñānamuṣṭi-mudrā*), and further holding the twelve great seals of the five mountain peaks, vajra, lotus, maṇi, karma, hook, noose, chain, bell, wisdom, sword, and Dharma wheel. His body rested upon a great white thousand-petaled lotus flower; his body was colored like the sun, and his five topknots radiated light. That light, having no master, pervaded the ten directions. With a smiling countenance, he then spoke this Great Victorious Vajraśekhara Supreme Reality Great Samaya Mantra, saying:
"Oṃ mahāvajrasenisa hūṃ traḥ hrīḥ aḥ hūṃ. Having spoken this mantra, he further spoke these verses:
"In the pure and wondrous lands of the ten directions, throughout the three times and the triple world, there is one most honored and peerless; this is the Great Wheel-Turning King."
It can crush the crowns of all Buddhas and gather all the Samyaksaṃbuddhas as its retinue;
by drawing near to it, one swiftly accomplishes the ground of great compassion.
If people of the final dharma age recite this mantra constantly, [they shall attain these benefits].
Weapons cannot harm them; fire and water cannot burn or sweep them away.
Padmapāṇi and Vajrapāṇi attend and guard them as their followers.
If one recites this one hundred and eight times, one can extinguish the sins of a hundred kalpas.
If one recites it one thousand times, one can fulfill all wishes;
if one recites it one lakṣa times, one attains the great vajra body;
if one recites it one koṭi times, one succeeds in becoming the Honored One Samantaprabha.
The thousand Buddhas come together to protect you; there is no doubt at all.
I shall now further explain the mudrā: it is the most supreme heart of the Vajra.
Firmly bind the ten fingers within; bend the *kṣānti* and *praṇidhi* fingers like the crown of the head.
This is called the Root Mind, the most supreme Cakra-mudrā.
If one constantly binds this seal, [one attains] the Honored One Vajrasattva,
the Lotus Maṇi King, and the Honored One Viśvakarman.
All the holy and venerable ones, Come together to increase their protection.
This person is like a vajra, Which no evils can destroy;
This body is like a mass of light, Able to shatter the darkness of the three realms.
This person is like a lotus flower, unsullied by any defilements;
this body is like karma, performing great deeds for the sake of all Buddhas;
this body is like the Honored One Samantabhadra, whom no Buddha can forsake.
With a body like Mañjuśrī, one can accomplish inexhaustible wisdom;
with a body like a vajra-wheel, one can turn the wheel of the principle-path.
By maintaining this mantra and mudrā, one can accomplish such matters as these.
Just as by relying on a pure place of contact, merely forming the supreme mudrā and reciting the root heart-mantra, there is nothing that is not accomplished;
whatever one performs is successful, and all aspirations are fulfilled.
The Vidyā for the Accomplishment of the Most Victorious Honored One, Vajraśekhara, says:
Oṃ vajrasattva guhya hūṃ. The Mantra for the Accomplishment of Vajrapāṇi, the Most Victorious Maṇi, says:
Oṃ vajraratna guhya traḥ. The Lotus Most Victorious Heart-mantra for the Accomplishment of Vajrapāṇi:
Oṃ vajradharmaghoṣa hūṃ. The mantra for accomplishing Vajrapāṇi, the supreme mind of skillful action:
Oṃ vajrakarmaghoṣa aḥ. The mantra for accomplishing the Vajra Hook, the supreme one who can hook:
Oṃ vajrasattvabandha ghuṣṭajaḥ. The mantra for accomplishing the Vajra Noose, the supreme one who can draw forth:
Oṃ vajraratnaprasāda hūṃ. The Vajra-Chain is accomplished; the Supreme One is able to bind.
Oṃ vajrapadmanamaḥ phaṭ vaṃ. The Vajra-Bell is accomplished; the Supreme One is able to gladden.
By holding the eight great vidyās, one can accomplish hundreds of thousands of deeds.
The mudrā is like the Vajradhātu; the mantra practitioner should know that for all those who are difficult to conquer, one should employ this mudrā and vidyā.
Furthermore, the secret words of the Vajrakhaḍga should be known as follows:
“It can destroy the city of ignorance and give birth to the wisdom of all Buddhas;
its seal is identical to that of Mañjuśrī, the *karma-samaya*.
Furthermore, listen to the secret mantra of the Vajracakra:”
“With two vajra-fists, the thumbs and ring fingers, and the index and middle fingers,
interlocking four times in this manner— this is called that secret mudrā.
If a practitioner of mantra does not construct a maṇḍala,”
By merely holding this seal and mantra, one is identical to the Greatly Established One;
all maṇḍalas and every limb of one’s own body become entirely an assembly of Buddhas— peerless and inconceivable.
There is no flavor superior to this.
Furthermore, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) should be explained through these secret words (*mantra*):
"As soon as one recites this mantra, the sixteen great bodhisattvas..."
Born from the Dharmadhātu, each holding their respective original insignia;
next, reciting the eight offerings and the mantras of the four means of attraction,
one immediately accomplishes the Great Perfect Mandala.
Next, recite the mantra of the *iṣṭadevatā*, the eight offerings, and the four means of attraction; the secret mantras shall now be explained:
"Furthermore, O Lord of Secrets, I shall further explain this most secret dharma of my heart, the very core of my mind: the Buddhas are known as the Five Yogas."
One should contemplate that the Universal Illuminator Lord is entirely identical to oneself.
Furthermore, one should visualize before oneself the Supreme Vajra Jewel,
abiding upon a blazing sun and holding a magnificent great jewel banner.
Next, on the right, one should again visualize the Vajra-lotus Hook, abiding upon a yellow wheel;
holding the hook, he has a great smile.
Next, on the left, one should likewise know the Vajra-jewel Great Treasury.
Abiding upon a green wheel, she holds a great round mirror.
Next, following after that, is the Great Passion Vajra Lotus;
abiding upon a red wheel, she holds a sublime great red lotus.
These are called the five yogas, the secret and most sublime flavor;
all that is desired shall be completely fulfilled.
Constantly performing this yoga, recite the eight great vidyās mentioned before.
Through the power of the secret mudrās, all one's aspirations shall be fully accomplished.
Without relying on invocations, mudrās, the recitation of mantras, incense, or flowers,
one shall attain the supreme siddhi and swiftly obtain it in this very life.
At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas and all the Vajradharas,
with single-minded attention, beheld the Buddha’s mind and dwelt in joy.

Chapter Nine: The Great Accomplishment of Vajraśrī At that time, Vajrasattva again, in the presence of all the Tathāgatas, spoke the heart-mantra of the Great Vajraśrī, the Mother of All Buddhas, who is the Eye of All Buddhas;
she gives birth to all phenomena and accomplishes everything.
This light can fulfill all aspirations, eliminate all inauspiciousness, generate all merit, and extinguish all transgressions.
It causes all sentient beings who behold it to rejoice, enables the understanding of the languages of all living beings,
and swiftly brings about the accomplishment of the *Uṣṇīṣa* of all families— supreme, peerless, and extraordinary.
Difficult to Conquer (Durjayā), it transcends the ten stages and encompasses all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and the Great Heavenly Kings.

It is capable of accomplishing all matters that are difficult to understand; its swiftness is unsurpassed, and it can fully accomplish the profound secrets of the five families, realizing them all simultaneously and in equal measure.

At that time, Vajrasattva, appearing suddenly before all the Tathāgatas, manifested in the form of the Mother of All Buddhas. He stood upon a great white lotus, his body radiant as the white moon, with a slight smile upon his two eyes. His two hands rested at his navel as if he had entered into *śamatha*.
From every limb, ten *nayuta-koṭi* Buddhas were born; to each and every Buddha he prostrated, honoring those from whom they had been born.

In a single instant, he simultaneously manifested as the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin, holding the wheel-seal (*cakramudrā*), emitting light from his crown, and gazing with a majestic eye while manifesting great supernatural powers. He returned to pay homage to the Mother of All Buddhas, the mantra from which he was born, reciting:
"May all the Uṣṇīṣa-mantras I have spoken bring about great accomplishment for all sentient beings through your grace, O Venerable One."
“I now only pray that the Venerable One will grant great auspiciousness so that this may be accomplished.
At that time, the Vajra Mother of All Buddhas, from whom she had originally arisen, looked auspiciously toward all directions and spoke the Root Vidyārāja:
*Namo bhagavate śrī-saḥ oṃ ruru svāhā ruru jvala tiṣṭha siddhalocanī sarvārthasādhani svāhā.* Then the Mother of Buddhas addressed all the Tathāgatas, saying:
“If there are those such as Vajraja or Vajraputra who constantly maintain this vidyā,
their bodies will be like a vajra mountain, like a vajra scepter, like the peak of a vajra, like the Tathāgata of the Vajradhātu,
like that Sattvavajra, like that Padmapāṇi, and like that Ākāśagarbha.”
Like Viśvakarman; like those four pāramitās, sixteen great bodhisattvas, four means of attraction, and eight great offerings;
like the mind of all buddhas; like the transformation bodies of all buddhas;
like the relics of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of buddhas; like the true body of the Buddha; like...
The Buddha’s every thought and all his activities are identical to those of all Tathāgatas; the words he utters immediately become mantras,
his movements and gestures of the limbs become great mudrās, the places his eyes behold become the Great Vajradhātu,
and the places his body touches become great mudrās.
If one constantly maintains this, one shall obtain such vajra-marks.

If one wishes to act as a great ācārya to instruct others in the mudrās and other secret dharmas, one must first recite this vidyā one thousand times; then all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Vajrasattvas will be fully delighted, all sentient beings who see one will regard them as their own parents, and one’s merit will be like that of a Wheel-Turning King, complete with the seven treasures, while one’s lifespan will endure for many millions of koṭis.

If one constantly maintains this vidyā, Vajrasattva and all the bodhisattvas will always follow and protect them; they shall attain great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and all their undertakings will be fully accomplished. In times of urgent distress, they will be like the sun rising in the sky; no heavy karmic obstructions from past lives, nor the seven planets or twenty-eight lunar mansions, can destroy them, and they shall attain great peace and happiness.
If one recites it one million times, one will attain the state of Great Nirvāṇa.

I shall now further explain the method of the maṇḍala of contemplative practice and secret mudrās: one should contemplate one’s own body as having the same form as mine, dwelling upon a great white lotus that gradually expands until it pervades the entire realm of space; or, by binding the root mudrā to empower oneself, one dwells in the samādhi of the Dharma-realm and shall swiftly attain the wisdom of all-knowledge.

As for the mudrā: with the two hands joined hollow-palmed, bend the two index fingers to rest upon the upper joints of the two middle fingers, forming the shape of a smiling eye; each of the two thumbs presses against the joint of the ring finger and the little finger, also forming the shape of a smiling eye; finally, the two little fingers are slightly parted, likewise forming the shape of a smiling eye. This is called the Fundamental Great Mudrā.

If one rubs the eyes and eyebrows with the mudrā, while simultaneously holding the fingers upright to wipe between the brows, one should visualize the formation of the five eyes. Then, reciting the vidyā while performing the mudrā, one wipes the face three times in a clockwise direction; all who see this will be filled with joy.

At that time, each of the Sarvabuddhoṣṇīṣarājas placed a vajra-wheel beneath the feet of the respective Mother of All Buddhas from whom they were born; thus two wheels were formed for each, one supporting her foot and the other covering the crown of her head.

Then all the Buddhas, the Wheel-Kings of the Uṣṇīṣa, made offerings and surrounded him, reciting one hundred and eight names of the sublime gāthā, the Great Vajra Auspiciousness, the Unsurpassed Victory, and praised it, saying:
"If one holds this King of Praises, By reciting it even once,
All Buddhas will gather like clouds, And the thirty-seven wisdoms will be perfected."
If one recites it twice, all Buddhas enter the body,
as do all the *avaśas* and the lords of the three realms.
If one recites the scripture three times, all dharmas are accomplished.
If one recites this sutra four times, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,
all that one does will be peaceful and secure.
If one recites this sutra five times, one will be revered and loved by humans and devas alike.
If one recites it six times, all sins can be extinguished.
If one recites it seven full times, immeasurable merit can be generated.
If one possesses *vajra* seeds and constantly maintains this King of Praises, all Buddhas will always provide protection.
Having spoken these words, the Great Vajra Śrī-Devī, who had previously arisen, further explained the method for painting the maṇḍala image:
"Take a clean, white cotton cloth and paint it to the size of one's own body; for all images within the yogas, one should always paint them seated at a size equal to one's own body."
Within this, one should paint three assemblies upon an eight-petaled lotus; in the center, paint my own body.
Directly in front of me, upon one lotus petal, paint the Sarvabuddhoṣṇīṣavijaya, holding an eight-spoked vajra-jewel wheel in his hand.
To the right of that, arrange the messengers of the seven planets in a clockwise direction.
In the second flower courtyard, one should paint Vajrasattva in front of the Cakravartin;
next, paint the eight great bodhisattvas, each holding their respective insignia.
Next, in the third flower courtyard, one should draw the eight Great Vidyārājas of the Eight Great Vajras, arranged clockwise.

Furthermore, on the four sides outside the flower courtyard, one should draw the eight offering goddesses and the messengers of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), all of whom wear lion crowns.
This is called the method for painting images.
The maṇḍala is also according to this same method. The Ācārya says:
"The eight great Bodhisattvas are as described in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* (Tantra of the Essential Principles); the eight Vajras are as explained in the *Sarvatathāgata-uṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*."

Furthermore, regarding the insignia of the eight offerings and the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), they are to be bestowed according to the distinct forms of the seven luminaries as described in the *Vajradhātu*.

Next, the method for performing the rite of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is explained: on the day when the lunar mansion Heart (*hṛdaya*), Willow (*pūrvaphalgunī*), Pleiades (*kṛttikā*), or Ox (*rohiṇī*) is in conjunction with the moon, one should not select for auspicious or inauspicious dates. On such a day of lunar mansion conjunction, one should fast for the duration of that single day and recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times. All one’s heart’s desires will be fulfilled at that very moment, and one will attain great *siddhi*. By performing the ritual before the altar of the image, one shall immediately achieve the manifestation of the Buddha-mother.
At that time, the Mother of the Buddha, Vajraśrī, again spoke the eight-syllable mantra for the accomplishment of the Great Compassionate Womb (Mahākaruṇā-garbha):
Ā VI RA HŪṂ KHAṂ HŪṂ HRĪḤ AḤ "If one recites this ten million times, one will attain the simultaneous and instantaneous realization of all dharmas within the Great Compassionate Womb."
The mudrā is like the bowl-mudrā of Śākyamuni.

Emerging from meditative concentration with this mudrā, rotate it and then bind the fundamental samaya-mudrā: join the two hands with palms hollowed and brought together at the heart; thus it is accomplished.
At that time, he further spoke the five-syllable vidyā-king for the accomplishment of the Noble Vajra Ākāśagarbha’s Summoning of Wealth:

VAṂ 1, HŪṂ 2, TRAḶ 3, HRIḤ 4, AḤ 5. The practitioner should draw the five great Vajra Ākāśagarbhas within a single luminous circle, each equal in size to his own body. Within that single circle, it is further divided into five; in the central circle, one should draw white Ākāśagarbha, holding a hook in his left hand and a jewel in his right.
In the front circle, paint yellow Ākāśagarbha, holding a hook in his left hand and grasping a jewel-vajra in his right.
In the right circle, paint blue Ākāśagarbha, holding a hook in his left hand and bearing a three-pronged jewel in his right, emitting great radiance.

In the subsequent circle, paint Ākāśagarbha in red; as before, he holds a hook in his left hand and a large red lotus in his right. In the circle to the left, paint Ākāśagarbha in blackish-purple; as before, he holds a hook in his left hand and a jewel-vajra (*ratnakarma*) in his right.
This is called the Rite of the Five Great Ākāśagarbhas for Seeking Wealth and Nobility.
If one paints this image, it should be painted upon blue or golden silk.
The Bodhisattva’s robes, crown, and necklaces should all follow their respective original colors, and he should be seated in the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).

Once this image has been painted, before the mandala, regardless of the time or direction, one should recite the five-syllable vidyā one hundred million times; one will then attain the accomplishment of wealth and nobility. By performing homa at regular intervals, one will swiftly obtain great siddhi.
Next, the mudrās shall be explained:
"The *samaya* of Viśvakarman consists of joining the earth-touching and wish-fulfilling fingers so that their tips meet like a needle;
this is known as the *samaya* secret seal of the Dharmadhātu-gaganagañja."
Next, extend the index fingers like three prongs; this is called the Vajra Ākāśagarbha.
Again, extend the index fingers in the shape of a jewel; this is called the Ratnaprabhāsa Ākāśagarbha.
Furthermore, bend the index fingers like lotus petals; this mudrā is named Padma Ākāśagarbha.
"Interlocking the fingers of the *śīla-mudrā* and the *vīrya-mudrā*—this is called the activity of Ākāśagarbha.
At that time, he further spoke the *vidyā-mantra* for the accomplishment of Vajraśrī: "Oṃ vajra śrī ma..."
HĀ ŚRĪ ĀNATIYA ŚRĪ SU MA ŚRĪ A GĪRAKA ŚRĪ MUDHA ŚRĪ.

This is the Vajraśrī-mudrā.
"Interlock the fingers at the joints, pressing the two thumbs together and extending them upward;
this is called the Seal for Destroying Planets and All Inauspiciousness.
One should visualize Mañjuśrī while performing the rite of subjugation."
"Form the mudrā and recite [the mantra] one hundred times; before long, you shall achieve accomplishment.

At that time, the Mother of All Buddhas from whom [he] had originally arisen again emitted hundreds of thousands of rays of multicolored light from the crown of her head. From within each ray of light, there emerged immeasurable vajras, brave and fiercely blazing; it was likewise so beneath her feet.
Then he spoke the mantra for accomplishing all vidyās:

"Oṃ tta tta tta tti tti tti tti tta tta tta vajrasattva jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ hrīḥ haḥ hūṃ phaṭ ṭhaḥ. "This mantra can accomplish all vidyās, can subjugate all devas, and can bring about the fulfillment of all tasks."

If one wishes to know future events, one should form the mudrā and place it against the left side of the body, reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, while maintaining the mudrā, one should sleep; the deity Āviśa will then appear in a dream and reveal all matters of good and ill fortune.
For this mudrā, form the Acala-kartri-mudrā with the hands of concentration and wisdom by interlacing the blades of the knives within the palms; thus it is accomplished.
If one wishes to recite any mantra, first recite this vidyā twenty-one times, and all will swiftly attain accomplishment.

If one wishes to travel to various regions, one should visualize one's previous physical form pressing down upon the soles of one's feet; by regarding oneself as the Honored One (Bhagavān), one will immediately attain unimpeded and unobstructed passage through all places, and all that one undertakes will be successfully accomplished.
This auspicious vidyā can accomplish hundreds of thousands of tasks; whatever the mind intends shall be fulfilled according to one's wishes.

Furthermore, there is a method wherein one uses lotus fiber as a lamp wick and fumigates it to produce smoke; by applying this to the point between the eyebrows, all *manuṣyas* will submit and be filled with affection and reverence.
Then the various Uṣṇīṣacakravartins each returned and entered into every single pore of the Sattvabuddhamātṛ, whereupon they suddenly vanished.
At that moment, the great assembly became silent all at once.
"Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi, I shall explain the inner homa,
which purifies solidified karma and causes one to attain the bodhicitta.
Seated upright, one forms a moon disc and contemplates the radiance of the syllable VAṂ."
The principal body has the form of a Buddha; with the Wisdom Fist abiding in compassion, this is called Śāntika, the inner homa of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, regarding the ritual of touching the earth, it is the Vajra-phrase of the causal syllable.
A fierce fire arises, burning away all inauspiciousness;
it is named the Vajra-Holder Ground, through which one swiftly awakens to peerless enlightenment.
Furthermore, the form of the granting of boons is like the syllable-mantra of the maṇi.
The light of jewels purifies the three karmas; the light of jewels destroys all karma.
This seal of the supreme samādhi is a phrase of pure, dustless clarity;
lustful defilements and all stains—the fetters and afflictions—are all rendered pure.
Karmaja uproots all states of existence; his speech is tranquil and unattached.
All that he is capable of doing results in the attainment of unimpeded, stainless tranquility.
Vajrapāṇi-sattva—these are called the five kinds of wisdom.
The Tathāgata’s Secret for Pacifying Calamities is the Great Compassion Pāramitā; Arising from the four immeasurable minds,
its mudrās and mantras correspond to the four Buddhas, And it is also called the Buddha’s Rite for Pacifying Calamities.
As soon as the slander was uttered once, all the Buddhas spoke in unison:
"This one is truly a son of the Buddha;
he can extinguish peerless offenses and can generate peerless merit."
Able to pacify the calamities of the three times, all Buddhas provide protection.
Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi, I shall further proclaim these secret mantra-words;
you should listen with a tranquil mind. These are the five kinds of Tathāgata wisdom.
And the four pāramitās.
Furthermore, listen with a single mind:
the mantra of Vajrasattva forms the fundamental karma-mudrā; from the seed-syllable, the vajra arises.
Filling that great realm of space, pervading this vajra fire,
it can summon all vajras and subjugate them as servants.
Furthermore, O Vajra King, through the samaya of one’s fundamental activity—
From the syllable HŪṂ arises the Great Hook, which universally hooks all things throughout the Dharma-realm;
all Buddhas of the ten directions come in their entirety to grant accomplishment,
so that whatever the heart desires, it shall be swiftly attained without limit.
Furthermore, O Vajrarāga, through the samaya of original karma,
the utterance of syllables gives rise to joy; its sound pervades the realms of the ten directions,
such that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas become wives of passionate love.
